thread.title: Apple's Valuation Elevated, No Thanks to iPhone, Says BMO

author: Barron's
title: Apple's Valuation Elevated, No Thanks to iPhone, Says BMO
text:
Apple 's ( AAPL ) stock is more expensive compared to where it has traded historically relative to the S&P 500 index, something that has more to do with buybacks than the iPhone , according to BMO Capital 's Tim Long .
In a note to clients today, Long, who has a Market Perform rating on the stock, raises his price target to $184 from $171, which is below the current price of $191.46, because he acknowledges that the P/E multiple on the shares has to go higher, essentially because of the company's "huge" capital returns program.
Long uses a multiple of 14 times his calendar 2019 EPS estimate for Apple of $13.14. That's up from his prior 13 times multiple. I would note that is a plain P/E, not adjusted for Apple's cash per share.
Long points out the stock is almost in line with the S&P 500's discount versus a big discount it historically had, and its because of the buybacks:
AAPL traded nearly at parity with the S&P back in 2014 (end of August hit ~99%) as excitement for the first large screen iPhones (iPhone 6 and 6 Plus) was building. AAPL is currently trading at only an 8% discount to the S&P (down from 17% three months ago), while on a three- and five-year historical average, it has typically traded at a 23% and 20% discount, respectively. We believe the stock is trading at a premium relative valuation based primarily on the huge stock buyback program.
Long's concern is that the next models of iPhone, presumably this fall, won't do much for the business, or the stock, as the average time mobile consumers take between upgrading their phones continues to stretch out:
We believe that the average iPhone replacement cycle was 3.2 years back at the end of CY2009 (only three models available, including 3G/3GS) before dropping to historical lows (2.2 years) five years later (CY2014) at the onset of the iPhone 6 cycle. Since then, the average replacement cycle has been hovering around the mid-two-year mark. We estimate that this rate is at 2.5 years but are concerned it could lengthen further without a compelling launch in September. Every 0.1-year change in replacement rate leads to 8 million units sold
Long believes China is Apple's most important market, and observes the iPhone's share there has been shrinking, now at about 6% of units sold among all vendors, as a result of a "combination of lack of compelling new devices and increased traction for local brands."
However, he does acknowledge Apple has had success with its non-iPhone products in the China market:
We believe that Apple could report Greater China (China, Hong Kong, Taiwan) revenues for the June quarter next week that are actually up on a y/y basis (still down, though, sequentially) given the "non-iPhone" portion of revenue, which we believe is outpacing iPhone revenue (Exhibit 4). We have been surprised over the past few quarters at how the China revenues have held up for Apple given what we believe has been a lackluster performance for iPhones. We think the biggest contributor on the "non-iPhone" portion is most likely the app store, but given the huge increase in this revenue bucket, we question the sustainability.
Apple will report quarterly results a week from tomorrow, July 31, after market close.
